title: Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule open a girls' school in Pune
text: Savitribai Phule, Jyotirao Phule and Sagunabai Kshirsagar started a school for girls at Bhide Wada in Pune, one of the first girls' schools started by Indians. Savitribai's colleague Fatima Sheikh later ran a school with her in the Sheikh family home. The written records about Fatima Sheikh are thin, and historians still debate the details.
why: Indian feminism begins with a Dalit-Bahujan woman and a Muslim woman claiming education against caste and patriarchy at the same time. Intersectionality is home-grown here, not imported. In 2023 the Supreme Court cleared the way for a national memorial at Bhide Wada.

sources.label: Savitribai Phule
Supreme Court allows national memorial to commemorate first girls' school in India
The evidence for Fatima Sheikh, and the dispute over it

title: Seneca Falls: the first women's rights convention in the US
text: At the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York, the first women's rights convention ended with 68 women and 32 men signing the Declaration of Sentiments, drafted by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and the M'Clintock family.
why: It happened in the same year the Phules opened their school in Pune. Feminism started in many places at once, not only in the West.

sources.label: The First Women's Rights Convention
Background: International Women's Day

title: Tarabai Shinde publishes 'Stri Purush Tulana'
text: Tarabai Shinde's Marathi pamphlet 'Stri Purush Tulana' (A Comparison of Women and Men) turned the tables on writers who blamed women. Every fault they pinned on women, she argued, men had too. It is one of the earliest modern feminist texts in India.
why: Calling out double standards has an Indian history of more than 140 years. The pamphlet was met with hostility and largely forgotten until it was republished in 1975, which is why a movement has to archive women's writing itself.

sources.label: Stri Purush Tulana
Tarabai Shinde: breaking caste and patriarchy glass ceilings

title: Pandita Ramabai opens Sharada Sadan, a home and school for widows
text: Pandita Ramabai was the first woman in India to earn the titles 'Pandita' and 'Sarasvati'. In 1889 she opened Sharada Sadan, where widowed girls and women could live and study. It began in Bombay and later moved to Pune.
why: Shelter, schooling and a route to independence under one roof, paid for partly with money she raised abroad. It is an early Indian model of a feminist organisation that both serves people and campaigns.

sources.label: Women's History Month 2020: Pandita Ramabai Sarasvati
Pandita Ramabai

title: New Zealand becomes the first self-governing country where women can vote
text: New Zealand's governor signed the Electoral Act, making it the first self-governing country where women could vote in parliamentary elections. It followed a petition of 31,872 signatures organised by Kate Sheppard and the Women's Christian Temperance Union.
why: Petitions plus persistence work. Māori and Pākehā women both voted in the elections that year.

sources.label: Suffrage petition submitted to Parliament on 28 July 1893
Women's suffrage in New Zealand

title: Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain imagines 'Ladyland'
text: Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain's 'Sultana's Dream' first appeared in The Indian Ladies' Magazine in Madras. It imagines Ladyland, a science-fiction world where women run everything and men are kept in seclusion, a mirror image of purdah.
why: Imagining the world you want is itself a political act. The story is among the earliest known Indian science fiction in English, and a model for creative, speculative feminist work.
place: Published in Madras; author from Bengal

sources.label: Sultana's Dream by Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain (review)
Sultana's Dream

title: The first International Women's Day
text: A year after socialist women meeting in Copenhagen agreed to hold an international women's day, the first celebrations took place in several European countries and the US. Marchers demanded the vote, the right to work and an end to discrimination at work.
why: International Women's Day began as a working women's protest, not a branding day. Worth remembering every 8 March.

sources.label: Background: International Women's Day

title: Petrograd women strike for 'bread and peace'
text: Women in Petrograd went on strike for 'bread and peace' on 8 March (23 February in Russia's old calendar). Days later the Tsar abdicated, and the new provisional government later granted women the vote.
why: This strike is why International Women's Day falls on 8 March. Women's economic protest helped topple an empire.

sources.label: Background: International Women's Day

title: The Women's Indian Association is founded, and women ask for the vote
text: The Women's Indian Association was founded in Adyar, Madras. That December an all-women delegation asked the Montagu–Chelmsford inquiry to give Indian women the vote. The request was turned down.
why: It was the first organised campaign for Indian women's suffrage. The vote then came step by step, province by province, starting with Madras and Bombay in 1921. Rights came from persistent organising, not one event.

sources.label: The Women's Indian Association and Indian constitutional thought
Women's suffrage in India

title: The All India Women's Conference meets for the first time
text: The All India Women's Conference was founded in 1927. Its first meeting, at Fergusson College in Poona, drew about 2,000 people to push for girls' education and women's welfare.
why: A national federation of local women's groups that still exists almost a century later. Its centenary in 2027 is a ready-made moment for public memory.

sources.label: History
All India Women's Conference

title: Women break the salt law
text: Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay led women to Chowpatty beach in Bombay to make salt against British law, and was among the first women arrested. Later that year Sarojini Naidu led the protest at the Dharasana salt works.
why: Mass civil disobedience made women visible as political actors in public space. Today's protest culture makes the same move.

sources.label: The Chowpatty Satyagraha
Women of Dandi March

title: Aruna Asaf Ali raises the flag at Gowalia Tank
text: The morning after the Quit India resolution, with the top leaders arrested and gatherings banned, Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag of the freedom movement at Gowalia Tank Maidan in Bombay. Police used lathis and tear gas on the crowd.
why: A movement survives the arrest of its leaders when others are ready to step up. A lesson in shared leadership, and in a woman taking the lead.

sources.label: Quit India (Gandhi Comes Alive)
Aruna Asaf Ali: brave heart of the Quit India movement
Aruna Asaf Ali

title: Fifteen women help write India's Constitution
text: Fifteen women sat in the Constituent Assembly that debated India's Constitution, among them Dakshayani Velayudhan, its only Dalit woman member. The others included Ammu Swaminathan, Durgabai Deshmukh, Hansa Mehta, Rajkumari Amrit Kaur and Sarojini Naidu.
why: Women were co-authors of the Republic. 'Founding mothers' is a constitution-first identity that belongs to everyone.

sources.label: These are the 15 women who helped draft the Indian Constitution
Dakshayani Velayudhan

title: Hansa Mehta helps make the Universal Declaration say 'human beings'
text: When the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris, Article 1 said 'All human beings are born free and equal'. The change from 'all men' is widely credited to India's delegate, Hansa Mehta.
why: Words are policy. An Indian woman helped make the world's rights charter include women, an ancestor of today's arguments about inclusive language.

sources.label: Women who shaped the Universal Declaration
Universal Declaration of Human Rights

title: The Constitution gives every adult an equal vote
text: When the Constitution came into force, Article 326 based elections on adult suffrage. Women voted as equals in the first general election of 1951–52, when about 173 million voters were registered.
why: Indian women did not have to win the national vote separately. But equal votes did not bring women an equal share of seats, which is why the reservation story runs all the way to 2026.

sources.label: Universal adult franchise: a brief constitutional history
Constitution of India

title: SEWA becomes a union for self-employed women
text: The Self Employed Women's Association, founded by labour lawyer Ela Bhatt in Ahmedabad, was registered as a trade union. It organised women such as vegetable vendors and waste-recyclers, who were outside the reach of existing unions.
why: Feminism as economic infrastructure: organising women in informal work. A model for moving from research to action.

sources.label: History
Self Employed Women's Association

title: Chipko: village women stand between the loggers and their forest
text: Chipko began when villagers at Mandal in the Himalayan hills turned back loggers on 24 April 1973. On 26 March 1974 (some accounts say 25 March), Gaura Devi led 27 women of Reni village to face down the contractors and save their forest.
why: Ecofeminism from India's hills. Rural women defended forests as their livelihood, linking climate justice and feminism decades before school climate strikes. The story often centres men; it should start with Gaura Devi.

sources.label: Chipko movement

title: 'Towards Equality' shows how far women had been left behind
text: The government-appointed Committee on the Status of Women in India published its report, 'Towards Equality'. It found that independent India had left many women behind, and it drew attention to a falling sex ratio.
why: Research turning into a movement: the report is often said to have laid the foundation of the modern Indian women's movement. Members Vina Mazumdar and Lotika Sarkar dissented when the committee rejected reserved seats for women in legislatures, a debate that ended with the 2023 Act.

sources.label: Towards Equality
Vina Mazumdar

title: Iceland's women take the day off, and do it again in 2023
text: About 90% of Iceland's women walked off their jobs and their housework for a day. On 24 October 2023, women and non-binary people, including the prime minister, held a full-day strike against the pay gap and gender-based violence.
why: The strike showed how much the country depended on women's work. In 1980 Iceland elected Vigdís Finnbogadóttir, the first woman in the world to be democratically elected president.

sources.label: 50 years ago, the women of Iceland took a day off, and inspired the world
Women, nonbinary people in Iceland strike for 24 hours to fight gender pay gap

title: The Mathura case sparks India's first national campaign on consent
text: The Supreme Court acquitted two policemen accused of raping a tribal teenager in a police station. In 1979 four law professors wrote an open letter, women's groups organised, and in 1983 Parliament changed the law on rape.
why: The template for consent politics: an open letter, new feminist groups such as the Forum Against Rape (1980), street protest and law reform working together. The 1983 law said that in custodial rape cases, courts should presume a survivor did not consent if she says so.

sources.label: Tuka Ram and Anr vs State of Maharashtra (judgment)
Mathura rape case
sources.note: Wikipedia dates the judgment to 1979; the judgment record says 15 September 1978.

title: The UN adopts CEDAW, the women's bill of rights
text: The UN General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women by 130 votes to none. It came into force in 1981, and India ratified it on 9 July 1993.
why: International law that Indian courts can and do use: the Supreme Court drew on CEDAW when it wrote the Vishaka guidelines in 1997.

sources.label: Status of treaties: CEDAW
Short history of the CEDAW Convention

title: Shah Bano wins maintenance in the Supreme Court
text: In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum, the Supreme Court held that a divorced Muslim woman who could not support herself could claim maintenance under Section 125 of the general criminal-procedure law.
why: It shows how women's rights get caught between personal law, religion and party politics. Parliament's 1986 response, the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, was criticised for diluting the ruling. Rights claims need to stand beyond party lines.

sources.label: Mohd. Ahmed Khan vs Shah Bano Begum (judgment)
Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum

title: One-third of local council seats are reserved for women
text: The 73rd and 74th Amendments to the Constitution, passed in 1992 and in force in 1993, reserved at least one-third of seats in village panchayats and town councils for women. By January 2025 about 14 lakh women were elected panchayat members, 46% of the total.
why: Proof that reservation changes who holds power, and the strongest evidence for the 2023 law on seats in Parliament.

Decentralisation @75: how the third-tier institutions have deepened India's democracy
National Panchayati Raj Day

title: Beijing: 189 countries sign up to a women's rights roadmap
text: At the Fourth World Conference on Women, 189 countries unanimously adopted the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action. It covers 12 critical areas, from poverty and violence to the media and the girl child.
why: Still the main global yardstick. It names 'women in power and decision-making' and 'the girl child' as priorities, the two themes closest to a Gen Z political mission.

sources.label: Fourth World Conference on Women
World conferences on women

title: Bhanwari Devi's fight leads to the Vishaka guidelines
text: Bhanwari Devi, a worker in Rajasthan's Women Development Programme, reported being gang-raped in 1992 for trying to stop a child marriage. Women's groups took the issue to the Supreme Court, which laid down India's first binding rules against sexual harassment at work.
why: A grassroots worker's courage created rights for every working woman in India. The Court drew on CEDAW, so global and local feminism reinforced each other.

sources.label: Vishaka and Ors vs State of Rajasthan (judgment)
Vishakha and Others v. State of Rajasthan

title: India's domestic violence law comes into force
text: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 came into force. It recognised physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse at home, and gave women civil remedies such as protection orders.
why: It made the personal legally political. Abuse at home, including control of money, became something a woman could take to court without having to start a criminal case.

sources.label: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005

title: Delhi's December protests rewrite the law on sexual violence
text: After a young woman was gang-raped and murdered on a Delhi bus, students and young people filled Raisina Hill and India Gate. The Justice Verma Committee took public suggestions and reported on 23 January 2013, and the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013 added offences such as stalking, voyeurism and acid attack.
why: Youth-led street protest, plus public suggestions sent to a committee, changed national law in under four months. The Act did not adopt the committee's call to end the marital-rape exception, which is still a live demand.

sources.label: Justice Verma Committee report summary

title: The POSH Act turns the Vishaka rules into law
text: The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, passed in April 2013, came into force. It made complaints committees at workplaces a legal duty and replaced the 1997 Vishaka guidelines.
why: It took 16 years to get from a grassroots worker's case to a statute. A win in court needs a follow-through campaign to become law.

sources.label: Government notifies prevention of sexual harassment law; Act has come into force from 9 December 2013

title: Ni Una Menos: 'not one woman less'
text: After the femicide of 14-year-old Chiara Páez and a tweet by radio journalist Marcela Ojeda, about 200,000 people marched in Buenos Aires under the slogan Ni Una Menos (estimates go up to 300,000). It became a movement across Latin America and beyond.
why: Hashtag to street to an annual mobilisation. Also a warning: the movement's own website domain has since lapsed, so public memory needs archives a movement owns.

sources.label: Ten years of Ni Una Menos: how one tweet led to a global phenomenon
Ni Una Menos website, as archived in 2019
sources.note: The domain no longer resolves (checked 24 Oct 2026).

title: Pinjra Tod: students say 'break the cage'
text: Women students covered Jamia Millia Islamia and nearby hostels in Delhi with 'Pinjra Tod' ('break the cage') posters, starting a campaign against hostel curfews that locked women in at night.
why: A campus campaign about women's right to the city and to public space at night, the same idea that powered Reclaim the Night in 2024.

sources.label: #PinjraTod gives voice to Indian women fed up with draconian university hostel rules

title: #MeToo goes global
text: The actor Alyssa Milano asked people who had been sexually harassed or assaulted to reply 'me too'. The hashtag spread worldwide, building on a movement the activist Tarana Burke had founded in 2006.
why: The defining Fourth Wave tool: survivor testimony at scale, online. It also shows how easily founders get erased, so credit Burke.

sources.label: History and inception
MeToo movement

title: #MeTooIndia: women speak up, and a court backs their right to
text: From late September 2018, actors and women journalists in India publicly named harassers, and a Union minister resigned on 17 October. On 17 February 2021 a Delhi court acquitted journalist Priya Ramani of criminal defamation, holding that the right to reputation cannot be protected at the cost of the right to dignity.
why: Online testimony moved into newsrooms and courtrooms. The Ramani ruling, which also said a woman can raise a grievance even decades later, is a shield for survivors who speak out.

sources.label: Government official resigns as #MeToo movement gathers force in India
Delhi court acquits Priya Ramani in criminal defamation case

title: The Sabarimala verdict and Kerala's 620 km Women's Wall
text: The Supreme Court ruled that women aged 10 to 50 could not be kept out of the Sabarimala temple. On 1 January 2019 lakhs of women formed a 620 km human chain across Kerala, from Kasaragod to Thiruvananthapuram, organised by the state government.
why: Equality versus custom inside faith is a live question, and the chain showed how many women can be mobilised in a single day. The verdict is under review: a nine-judge bench began hearing a wider reference in April 2026.

sources.label: Indian Young Lawyers Association vs The State of Kerala (judgment)
Kerala's wall of resistance: lakhs of women stand up against patriarchy
Supreme Court Constitution bench begins hearing on women's entry at Sabarimala

title: Shaheen Bagh: a women-led sit-in in Delhi
text: Women in Delhi's Shaheen Bagh, including older women nicknamed the 'dadis', held a round-the-clock road sit-in against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act. It lasted about 101 days, until police cleared it during the Covid-19 lockdown.
why: It changed who leads protest: homemakers and grandmothers became national political figures, and Bilkis made TIME's 100 list in 2020. The Supreme Court later ruled that public roads cannot be occupied indefinitely, which shapes how protest can be organised.

sources.label: After a 101-day sit-in, Shaheen Bagh protest cleared due to coronavirus lockdown

Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police

title: Woman, Life, Freedom: Iran rises after Jina Mahsa Amini's death
text: Jina Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Iranian-Kurdish woman, died in the custody of Iran's morality police. Protests followed under the slogan 'Woman, Life, Freedom', and a UN fact-finding mission later found the state responsible for her unlawful death.
why: Young women led a mass uprising under an openly feminist slogan, the clearest 2020s example of feminism as a mass political movement.

sources.label: Iranian government 'bears responsibility' for Amini's death, brutal crackdown, UN mission says

title: Parliament passes the Women's Reservation Act
text: The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, called the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, received the President's assent. It reserves one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha, the state assemblies and the Delhi Assembly for women, including within the seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
why: The 1974 dissent in 'Towards Equality' finally became law. But the reservation only starts after a census and a redrawing of constituencies, so 'when does it start?' became the next question.

sources.label: President gives assent to India's historic women's reservation bill
President Droupadi Murmu grants assent to Women's Reservation Bill

title: Reclaim the Night: women take Bengal's streets at midnight
text: A postgraduate trainee doctor was raped and murdered on duty at Kolkata's RG Kar Medical College; her body was found on 9 August. From 11:55 pm on 14 August, the eve of Independence Day, thousands of women marched across West Bengal in the 'Reclaim the Night' protests.
why: One social-media call, started by Rimjhim Sinha, became a statewide night protest demanding safety at work and in public space at night. The marches were overwhelmingly peaceful.

sources.label: Kolkata doctor rape-murder: women fill streets across West Bengal in midnight protests
Indian women lead night protests after doctor's rape and murder

title: Gisèle Pelicot makes 'shame change sides'
text: Gisèle Pelicot refused a closed-door trial so that the public could see the case against 51 men, including the husband who admitted drugging her so that she could be abused. A court in Avignon convicted every one of them.
why: By choosing to be visible, a survivor flipped the stigma onto the perpetrators. Her rallying idea, that shame must change sides, became a global talking point on consent.

sources.label: With guilty verdicts, victim's rape ordeal in France becomes a message of hope
A French rape victim goes public. She makes 'shame change sides.'

title: Women's reservation is in force, but still waiting to start
text: On 16 April 2026 the government brought the 2023 Women's Reservation Act into force. The next day, a constitutional amendment that would have let the quota start after a redrawing of seats based on the 2011 census failed in the Lok Sabha: 298 for, 230 against, short of the two-thirds needed. The one-third quota still waits for a redrawing of seats after the next census.
why: The unfinished business of Indian feminism. Seventy-six years after equal votes, reserved seats for women are law but not yet working, which gives young voters a concrete demand they can track.

sources.label: Lok Sabha rejects Constitution (131st) Amendment Bill 2026; Centre withdraws Delimitation Bill
The Delimitation Bill, 2026

title: 2026: the UN International Year of the Woman Farmer
text: The UN General Assembly declared 2026 the International Year of the Woman Farmer, to raise awareness of women's central role in food systems and to tackle the barriers they face.
why: It brings rural and working-class women into the 2026 conversation, and it is a hook for research on women in Indian farming.

sources.label: FAO welcomes the celebration of the International Year of the Woman Farmer in 2026
